facts.statement: Dyrosaurus is an extinct genus of crocodylomorph that lived during the Early Eocene.
facts.quote: Dyrosaurus is a genus of extinct crocodylomorph that lived during the Early Eocene.

facts.statement: The name Dyrosaurus is derived from the Greek word for lizard or reptile and the mountain Djebel Dyr near the discovery site of the type species.
facts.quote: The name Dyrosaurus comes from sauros (σαῦρος) the Greek for lizard or reptile, and Dyr for Djebel Dyr (mountain) close to where the type species was discovered.

facts.statement: French paleontologist Auguste Pomel named the genus Dyrosaurus in 1894 after Djebel Dyr mountain in Algeria, where fossilized vertebrae were found in a phosphate mine.
facts.quote: French paleontologist Auguste Pomel named the genus Dyrosaurus in 1894 for Djebel Dyr, a mountain near Tebessa in Algeria where its fossilised vertebrae were found in a phosphate mine.

facts.statement: The first remains of Dyrosaurus were originally named Crocodilus phosphaticus by Thomas in 1893 based on Early Eocene fossils from Gafsa, Tunisia.
facts.quote: The first remains of Dyrosaurus were named Crocodilus phosphaticus by Thomas (1893) for Early Eocene crocodyliform remains from Gafsa, Tunisia.

facts.statement: Giuseppe de Stefano named the family Dyrosauridae in 1903, referencing the holotype locality in Djebel Dyr, Algeria.
facts.quote: In 1903, the family Dyrosauridae was named by Giuseppe de Stefano referring to the locality for the holotype was found in Djebel Dyr, Algeria.

facts.statement: Thévenin recognized in 1911 that Dyrosaurus phosphaticus was a Lower Eocene crocodyliform based on better preserved material.
facts.quote: Thévenin (1911a, 1911b), with some better preserved material, recognized that Dyrosaurus phosphaticus was a Lower Eocene crocodyliform.

facts.statement: D. phosphaticus fossils have been found in Algeria and Tunisia, while D. maghribensis fossils have only been found in Morocco.
facts.quote: D. phosphaticus was first discovered in Algeria and Tunisia whereas D. maghribensis has only been found in Morocco.

facts.statement: The type species D. phosphaticus had thin jaws with numerous recurved teeth, indicating a predominantly fish-eating diet similar to the modern Gharial.
facts.quote: La especie tipo D. phosphaticus, cuyos restos fueron encontrados en países como Argelia y Túnez, posee mandíbulas delgadas con numerosos dientes recurvados, indicadores de una dieta predominantemente ictiófaga (similar al moderno gavial de la India).

facts.statement: Dyrosaurus teeth had a smooth enamel layer and were long and frequently sharp, helping it hunt fast-moving prey.
facts.quote: Los dientes de Dyrosaurus poseen una suave capa de esmalte y son largos y frecuentemente agudos, ayudándolo a cazar a presas de rápidos movimientos.

facts.statement: Initially, scarce remains prevented further understanding of the animal's anatomy.
facts.quote: Sin embargo, los escasos restos no permitían saber más acerca de la anatomía de este animal.

facts.statement: Stable isotopic and paleohistological analysis indicates Dyrosaurus was ectothermic, with body temperature, metabolic rate, bone tissue morphology, and red blood cell dimensions similar to modern crocodilians.
facts.quote: El análisis isotópico estable y paleohistológico indica que el Dyrosaurus era ectotérmico, con una temperatura corporal, una tasa metabólica, una morfología del tejido óseo y unas dimensiones de los glóbulos rojos similares a las de los cocodrilos actuales, lo que concuerda con la hipótesis de que los neosuquios eran ancestralmente ectotérmicos.

facts.statement: It is likely that Dyrosaurus shared a lifestyle similar to modern crocodylomorphs.
facts.quote: Por lo tanto, es probable que compartiera un estilo de vida similar al de los cocodrilomorfos modernos.

facts.statement: Dyrosaurus belongs to the family Dyrosauridae.
Dyrosaurus is classified within the superorder Crocodylomorpha.
Dyrosaurus is part of the unranked family Neosuchia.
The Paleobiology Database lists the time range for Dyrosaurus as Albian to Priabonian (113.2 to 33.9 million years ago).
facts.quote: Time range: Albian to Priabonian (113.2 to 33.9 million years ago)

rejected.statement: Dyrosaurus was a large reptile with an estimated body length of 6.5 meters.
rejected.quote: It was a large reptile with an estimated body length of 6.5 m.
